extracted.intended_audience: college and university administrators, Title IX coordinators, and higher-education counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize legal standards and institutional obligations for postsecondary institutions in light of the January 9, 2025 federal court vacatur of the 2024 Title IX Regulations, and identify what procedures and state-law duties remain in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory meaning of 'discrimination on the basis of sex' under Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court concluded that under Title IX, 'discrimination on the basis of sex' means 'discrimination on the basis of being a male or female,' as distinguished from 'gender identity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Court determined the statutory text provides only that recipients may not treat a person worse than another similarly situated individual on the basis of a person's sex (i.e., male or female), a regulatory expansion to include gender identity exceeded the agency's authority in the Court's view. Institutions should interpret Title IX compliance obligations with this textualist reading in mind unless and until appellate or other binding decisions say otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) limits on agency rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court determined the USDOE exceeded its authority under the APA by defining 'discrimination on the basis of sex' to include gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations must be within the agency's statutory authority and follow APA procedures; agencies that advance interpretations beyond what statute authorizes risk vacatur. Institutions should monitor whether agency actions are procedurally and substantively defensible before relying on new regulatory interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment / compelled speech concern
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court found that requiring recipients 'to use names and pronouns associated with a student's asserted gender identity' violated the First Amendment right to free speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates compelling specific speech (e.g., mandated use of particular pronouns) may be subject to constitutional challenge; institutions should weigh compelled-speech risks and seek legal guidance on how to handle names/pronouns in policy and practice consistent with constitutional limits and applicable state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spending Clause vagueness and overbreadth constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court determined the 2024 regulations were unconstitutionally vague and overbroad in violation of the Spending Clause because recipients 'have no way of predicting what conduct will violate the law.' The Spending Clause requires conditions on federal funds to be unambiguous and not induce unconstitutional action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions attached to federal funding must be stated with sufficient clarity so recipients can conform their conduct; vague or overbroad regulatory conditions risk invalidation. Institutions relying on conditional federal-funding requirements should ensure policies are sufficiently definite or seek clarification from the Department of Education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary and capricious standard (reasoned decisionmaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court opined that defining 'discrimination on the basis of sex' to include 'gender identity' was arbitrary and capricious, noting inconsistencies in the Department's reasoning (e.g., permitting sex separation in certain contexts but deeming sex separation harmful in others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency rules must be reasoned and consistent; where an agency's rationale is inconsistent with statutory context or prior practice, courts may find rulemaking arbitrary and capricious. Institutions should be cautious about relying on agency interpretations that appear inadequately explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability considerations in regulatory invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court considered but rejected severing only the directly challenged parts of the 2024 regulations, concluding the definition of sex 'permeates virtually every provision' and therefore vacated the entirety of the 2024 Title IX Regulations (excepting a few unrelated provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a core regulatory definition underpins many provisions, courts may vacate the entire rule rather than sever discrete parts. Institutions should assume broad effects of vacatur where a central definition is implicated and prepare for reversion to prior regulatory regimes unless an appellate court rules otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of nationwide vacatur on enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: By determining vacatur was the appropriate remedy, the Court decided the 2024 Title IX Regulations, in their entirety, are invalid and must be set aside nationwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vacatur removes a regulation from effect nationally; institutions should treat the vacated rule as no longer in force and re-evaluate policies and processes that were implemented based on the vacated regulation. Continue to monitor for appeals or further agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion to the most recent prior regulations (practical effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Court did not explicitly state the 2020 Title IX Regulations would automatically return, the Court's vacatur of the 2024 regulations means the most recent prior set (the 2020 regulations) appears to be the operative framework unless changed by future action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions that changed procedures to comply with the 2024 regulations should plan to revert to or reassess compliance with the 2020 regulations (for example, live-hearing requirements), subject to legal advice and any transitional guidance from the Department of Education.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2020 Title IX live-hearing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 Title IX Regulations required colleges and universities to conduct live hearings; the 2024 regulations allowed other options (e.g., single investigator model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions that adopted investigator-only or other non-live-hearing models under the 2024 regulations may need to resume live-hearing procedures consistent with the 2020 regulations. Institutions should consult counsel about how to handle ongoing matters and whether to modify hearing procedures immediately or await further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued applicability of California anti-discrimination laws
rubrics_metrics.description: California law expressly prohibits discrimination not only on the basis of 'sex' but also on the basis of gender, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation, and defines prohibited sexual harassment more broadly than the 2020 Title IX regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with federal vacatur, California institutions must comply with state statutes and regulations (including broader definitions and protections). Policies should be aligned with state law obligations regardless of federal regulatory changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: SB 493 grievance-procedure and definition requirements (California)
rubrics_metrics.description: SB 493 (effective January 1, 2021) clarified definitions in Education Code section 66262.5 regarding sexual harassment and provided a new grievance procedure set forth in Education Code section 66281.8; many colleges updated policies in light of SB 493.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: California colleges and universities should ensure their grievance procedures and definitions conform to SB 493 requirements and consult legal counsel about compliance in light of the federal vacatur. Institutions that have not updated policies should do so promptly to meet state-law obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations regarding pregnancy and lactation accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: Colleges and universities must continue to comply with state and federal law regarding pregnancy and lactation accommodations for employees and students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protections and accommodation requirements for pregnancy and lactation remain in effect notwithstanding changes to Title IX regulations; institutions must maintain compliant policies and practices and cannot rely on vacatur to relax these obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical institutional guidance and need for counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alert advises colleges and universities currently processing Title IX matters under the 2024 regulations to consult legal counsel as to how to continue processing those matters in light of the Court's ruling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should seek immediate legal advice to determine how to handle ongoing investigations/hearings, whether to pause, convert, or continue proceedings, and how to update policies and training. Expect possible Department of Education guidance and changes under a new administration; plan for transitional compliance steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipated administrative/regulatory action under incoming administration
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more likely that the incoming administration will affirm implementation of the 2020 Title IX Regulations upon inauguration; the USDOE may issue guidance to clarify practical aspects of the vacatur, and issuing new regulations is likely to be a lengthy process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should prepare for the 2020 regulations to be in effect and for potential short-term guidance from the Department of Education rather than rapid promulgation of new federal rules. Continue monitoring federal and state developments and update compliance plans accordingly.
